doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Sesame Street tuba and studying with Nadia Boulanger with Joe Raposo
summary: Raph played the tuba for Telly Monster. He recalls studying with Boulanger in 1956 and playing army base gigs with Joe Raposo.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I see you’ve worked on “Sesame Street?”

Yeah. I never did it as a steady job but they have a character there called Telly monster. And he plays — they call it a tuba, it turns out to be like an E flat alto horn that’s all smashed up and he kind of holds it while a tuba player plays the tuba. And I was the tuba player on many occasions. So a lot of the episodes where Telly monster has some sort of carryings on about playing tuba or dropping it or losing it or whatever, the tuba that you hear is me. Joe Raposo and I were friends for years. We both studied with Nadia Boulanger back in 1956. That’s where I met Joe. In fact at that time we would take our private lesson with her, we would take a class lesson with her, we’d sit in the studio and play, and then at night there was a French and an English Army base, two different bases, in Fountainbleu, France. And I put together a little combo. And we used to go play these places. We’d make like six dollars a night or so. But it was something to do at night. Joe was the piano player.
Neat. I think Quincy took from her also.

I think he might have, yeah. He was with Dizzy Gillespie’s World Statesmen Band, and they went down to South America and the first place he went was over to Villa Lobos and he hung out with him. Quincy was always searching, always looking. Yeah, there ain’t much wrong with Quincy.
